scenes.title: Windowing, Joins & Watermarks
scenes.subtitle: Core patterns for stateful stream processing
scenes.narration: Windowing, joins, and watermarks are the foundational patterns that make sense of unbounded streams and out-of-order events.

scenes.title: Types of Windows
bullets: Sliding: fixed size, overlapping, stepping forward
Session: dynamic windows split by gaps of inactivity
Windows group unbounded data into finite chunks
scenes.narration: Windows carve an endless stream into finite chunks you can aggregate. Tumbling windows are fixed, non-overlapping intervals like each minute. Sliding windows have a fixed size but overlap, advancing by a smaller step to smooth results. Session windows are dynamic, opening and closing around bursts of activity separated by gaps of inactivity, which suits user sessions.

scenes.title: Event Time vs Processing Time
steps: Arrives late or out of order
Watermark decides when to close a window
scenes.narration: Streams distinguish when an event happened from when it was processed. An event carries its own event-time timestamp. It travels through networks and buffers, so it may arrive late or out of order. A watermark is the engine's estimate of how far event time has progressed. When the watermark passes a window's end, the engine finalizes that window and emits its result.

scenes.title: Stream-Stream vs Stream-Table Joins
scenes.narration: Joins combine streams in two main ways. A stream-stream join matches events from two streams that fall within a time window, buffering state until events can pair up or expire. A stream-table join instead enriches each event by looking up the latest value in a table keyed by a common field, needing no window. Choosing correctly keeps state bounded and results accurate.

scenes.title: Windowed Aggregation with a Watermark
scenes.code:
# Spark: count per 5-min window, allow 2 min of lateness
(events
    .withWatermark('event_time', '2 minutes')
    .groupBy(window(col('event_time'), '5 minutes'))
    .count())

# Events later than the watermark are dropped
# State for closed windows is purged to bound memory
scenes.narration: This example counts events in five-minute event-time windows. The watermark of two minutes tells the engine to wait that long for late data before finalizing a window. Events arriving later than the watermark are dropped as too late. Just as importantly, the watermark lets the engine purge state for closed windows, keeping memory usage bounded on an infinite stream.

scenes.text: Watermarks trade a little latency for correctness with out-of-order data, and they bound state so long-running jobs never exhaust memory.
scenes.narration: The key insight is that watermarks trade a little latency for correctness with out-of-order data. Just as vitally, they bound state so long-running streaming jobs never exhaust memory.
